## JSP-000199 · For which n do planar crescent configurations exist?

| Field | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Date proposed | No later than 1983 (bibliographic evidence) |
| Mathematical area | Geometry / Distance geometry |
| Problem description | Determine the integers $n \ge 2$ for which a set of $n$ points in the Euclidean plane, with no three collinear and no four concyclic, realizes exactly $n-1$ distinct distances whose multiplicities are $1,2,\ldots,n-1$, each occurring once. Multiplicity counts unordered pairs of distinct points; the distances need not be ordered by size. Such a set is called a crescent configuration. Erdős conjectured that no such configurations exist for all sufficiently large $n$. |
| Current status | Open |
| Lean proof | No |
| Eligible to claim | No |
| Historical bounty |  |
| Elapsed years | About 43 years (since 1983) |
| Publication details | [Erdős Problem #217](https://www.erdosproblems.com/217) — problem statement and historical references.<br>Burt et al., [Crescent configurations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.07220) — arXiv:1509.07220 (2015), definitions of general position and crescent configurations.<br>Fish et al., [Crescent configurations in normed spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.08769) — arXiv:1909.08769 (2019), Section 1.1, the Euclidean formulation and its general-position restrictions. |
